title: Your First C# Program
description: Write and run your first C# console application.

data.text: Writing your first C# program is an exciting moment. In this lesson, you'll create a console application, understand its structure, and learn how to write output and accept input.

The classic first program prints 'Hello, World!' to the console. In C#, you use `Console.WriteLine()` to display text. With modern C# (9.0+), you can use top-level statements to skip the boilerplate class and Main method structure.

data.title: Hello World — Top-Level Statements
data.content: The simplest possible C# program using top-level statements

data.title: Top-Level Statements
data.text: Top-level statements were introduced in C# 9.0. They eliminate the need for boilerplate code, making C# approachable for beginners. The compiler automatically generates a class and Main method behind the scenes.

Before top-level statements, every C# program needed a class with a `Main` method. Understanding this structure is important because you will encounter it frequently in existing codebases and when you need more control over program execution.

data.title: Traditional Program Structure
data.content: Complete C# program with explicit class and Main method

data.title: Program Structure Breakdown
items: **using System;** — Imports the System namespace so you can use Console, String, and other core types without fully qualifying them.
**namespace MyFirstApp** — A container that organizes related classes. Namespaces prevent naming conflicts.
**class Program** — A class is a blueprint that groups related code. The Program class holds the Main method.

**static void Main(string[] args)** — The entry point. The CLR starts here. `static` means it belongs to the class (not an instance). `void` means it returns nothing. `args` receives command-line arguments.
**Console.WriteLine()** — Outputs text to the console window.
**Console.ReadLine()** — Waits for the user to type text and press Enter.

data.text: String interpolation lets you embed expressions directly inside string literals using the `$` prefix. It's cleaner and more readable than string concatenation with the `+` operator.

data.title: String Interpolation Examples
data.content: Different ways to format strings in C#

data.title: Verbatim Strings
data.text: Use `@"..."` for verbatim strings that preserve whitespace and backslashes. Use `@$"..."` or `$@"..."` for verbatim interpolated strings. Useful for file paths like `@"C:\Users\Name\file.txt"`.
Interactive programs read user input with `Console.ReadLine()`, which returns a string. You often need to convert this string to other types (int, double, bool) for calculations.

data.title: Reading and Converting Input
data.content: Reading user input and converting to different types

data.title: Parse vs TryParse
data.text: `int.Parse()` throws an exception if the input is not a valid number. `int.TryParse()` safely returns false instead. Always prefer TryParse for user input to avoid crashes.

data.title: Console Output Options
items: `Console.WriteLine(value)` — Outputs value followed by a newline
`Console.Write(value)` — Outputs value without a newline (stays on same line)

data.title: Exercise: Interactive Greeter
data.description: Build a program that interacts with the user and provides personalized output.
steps: Create a new console project: `dotnet new console -n InteractiveGreeter`
In Program.cs, prompt the user for their name with `Console.Write()`
Use string interpolation to print a personalized greeting
Prompt for their favorite color and store it
Print a message like: "Nice to meet you, [name]! I like [color] too!"
Add validation: if the name is empty, print "Please enter a valid name." instead
data.expectedOutcome: A console app that takes two inputs from the user and prints personalized messages, with basic input validation.

items.text: Created a new console project with dotnet new
items.hint: Your project folder should contain Program.cs and a .csproj file

items.text: Used string interpolation with the $ prefix
Converted input strings to other types
Added comments to explain your code

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: C# programs can use top-level statements for simplicity
Console.WriteLine() outputs text; Console.ReadLine() reads input
String interpolation ($"...{var}...") is cleaner than concatenation
Always use TryParse for user input to avoid exceptions
Comments (//) help explain your code to others
data.takeaway: Your first C# program is just the beginning — now you can build interactive console applications.
